why: Lowest common ancestor via parent pointers: an iterative stack DFS records each node's parent, then p's ancestors go into a set and the first ancestor of q found in that set is the answer.
hints: If every node knew its parent, how would you find where the paths from p and q to the root first meet?
Traverse with an explicit stack and store parent[child] = node. Then walk from p to the root, adding each node to a set.
Walk up from q; the first node already in the set is the LCA. O(n) time and space. First rebuild children from the level-order strings (each non-null node consumes the next two slots).
pitfalls: A node is its own ancestor: include p itself in the set, and check q itself first.
p and q are values; map values to node positions.
In this level-order format null entries do not reserve child slots, so the 2i+1 formula is wrong.
constraints:
• Not stated in the source; reasonable bounds for practice:
  • 2 <= number of nodes <= 10^5
  • Node values are unique integers; p != q and both exist in the tree.
